Shopify Brand Identity for New Store Owners: Logo to Style Guide

By Marie Glow StudioUpdated September 23, 2026

It is common for new store owners to open Shopify, pick a theme and start uploading products, then hunt for a logo halfway through. It works, but it often leaves the store looking patched together: one color on the buttons, a different one in the banner, a font that changes from page to page. Settling your brand identity first prevents most of that, because every later decision has something to check against.

This guide explains why identity comes before the build, what each piece is for, and what to have ready before you begin. The basics of product branding post is a good companion if you want the fundamentals.

Why the order matters

Every store page asks you to make design choices: a button color, a heading font, the tone of a product description, the style of an image. If you have not decided these in advance, you decide them again on every page, and small differences pile up. Shoppers may not name what feels off, but a store that looks inconsistent feels less trustworthy. The post on why cohesive branding matters explains the trust side in more depth.

Deciding first also saves time. Once the identity exists, building the store becomes assembly rather than invention.

The pieces, in the order to make them

  1. Brand direction. Write a few words for how the brand should feel and who it is for. Everything else follows from this.
  2. Logo. A primary logo that stays readable small, such as in a browser tab or a social profile photo, and on a light and dark background.
  3. Colors. A small palette: usually a main color, an accent and a couple of neutrals. Check that text remains readable on every background you plan to use.
  4. Fonts. One font for headings and one for body text. Two is plenty.
  5. Style guide. One document that records all of the above, plus how to use it.
  6. Templates and graphics. Social graphics and other assets built from the guide.

What a style guide is actually used for

A style guide is not a nice extra. It is the reference you open when you have to make a decision at speed. Here is what it does for a store owner:

  • It keeps the store consistent. When you add a new collection banner or a sale graphic, you pull the exact colors and fonts from the guide instead of guessing.
  • It speeds up handoffs. If you hire a photographer, a virtual assistant or someone to make pins, the guide tells them what to do without a long explanation.
  • It prevents drift. Over a year, small tweaks add up. The guide shows what the brand looks like when it is right.
  • It supports your marketing. Pins, emails and social posts that share the same look are easier to recognize, and recognition builds over time. The branding versus marketing post explains how the two work together.

    • Common mistakes to avoid

    Picking a logo before knowing the brand direction, using too many colors, choosing a decorative font that is hard to read at small sizes, and copying a look that suits someone else's audience are the usual ones. The branding mistakes post covers more, and it is worth reading before you commission or design anything.

    What to have ready before you start

    • Your business name and the words that describe the feeling you want.
    • A few examples of styles you like and, just as useful, styles you do not.
    • Your product images, or the plan for them, so colors can be chosen to sit well with them.
    • A list of where the brand will appear first: the store, social profiles, packaging, pins.

    If you already have a store and are unhappy with how it looks, the redesign guide covers when to fix and when to rebuild. And if your products are handmade, the handmade brand guide shows how identity carries into story pages and product pages.

Frequently asked questions

Should I design my logo before building my Shopify store?

Yes, ideally. Deciding the logo, colors and fonts first means every page of the store is built from the same choices, instead of being decided again page by page. It usually saves time and produces a more consistent store.

What is a brand style guide used for?

A style guide records your logo, colors, fonts and how to use them. Store owners use it to keep new banners, pins and emails consistent, to brief designers or assistants quickly and to stop the look drifting over time.

How many colors and fonts should a new store use?

Keep it small. A palette of a main color, an accent and a couple of neutrals is usually enough, with one font for headings and one for body text. Fewer choices make the store look more consistent and are easier to keep up.
